label: Two homes

what_happens.title: What two homes means
goals: The grown-ups will live in two homes
It is a grown-up decision and not the child's fault
Both grown-ups keep loving the child
what_happens.parentSkill: Use one calm sentence both grown-ups agree on, like: 'We decided to live in two homes. It is a grown-up decision, and we both love you.'

who_is_there.title: Who is in my two homes
goals: Each grown-up looks after me at their home
Other family and friends stay in my life
Other kids live in two homes too
who_is_there.parentSkill: Name who will be at each home, including pets, siblings and any other adults, and keep other important people in the child's life.

what_i_do.title: What I do on switch days
goals: Use the calendar to know where I will be
Pack a travel bag with special things
Keep in touch with the other grown-up
what_i_do.parentSkill: Make a colour calendar together and let your child pack a travel bag with a comfort item that goes everywhere.

if_scared.title: If I feel sad or worried
goals: Sad, angry, worried and relieved feelings are all okay
It is not my fault and not my job to fix
Calm tools: talking, drawing, slow breaths, a hug
if_scared.parentSkill: Name and accept all feelings: 'You feel sad and angry. That makes sense. It is not your fault.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the switch day
goals: Make the calendar and pack the travel bag
Set up a little special spot in each home
rehearsal.parentSkill: Make the colour calendar together and let your child decorate their spot in each home.

steps: Grown-ups explain that they will live in two homes
Look at a calendar that shows the days at each home
Pack a bag with special things for the switch
Say goodbye at one home and hello at the other
Settle in: my bed, my toys and the routine at this home
Call or message the other grown-up, as agreed
Switch back on the next switch day
sensory: a bag that travels between homes
different smells and sounds in each home
a calendar with colours for each home
a car ride or walk on switch days
a heavy or quiet feeling in the chest
honestyNotes: Children often think the separation is their fault or that they can fix it; say clearly that it is a grown-up decision and not the child's fault, and never promise the grown-ups will get back together. Never blame either parent, never ask the child to pass messages or keep secrets, and never make the child choose sides. Let the parent explain the reason in their own words.

fallbackAnswer: No. It is a grown-up decision, and it is not because of anything you did or said.
Nothing you do could cause it or fix it.

questionButtons.text: Do you both still love me?
fallbackAnswer: Yes. Both your grown-ups love you, and that never changes.
Grown-ups can stop living together, but they never stop loving their kids.
That is a grown-up decision, and [[GROWNUP]] will be honest with you.
It is okay to wish for it, and to talk about that wish.
You will have days at each home, and the calendar shows which.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you the plan.

questionButtons.text: Will my things be at both homes?
fallbackAnswer: You will have a bed and some things at each home.
Your travel bag carries the special things.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you where the pet lives.
You can visit and help look after it.

questionButtons.text: Can I still see my other grown-up?
fallbackAnswer: Yes. The calendar shows the days, and you can keep in touch in between, as agreed.
Both grown-ups want to see you.

questionButtons.text: Do I have to tell my friends?
fallbackAnswer: You can choose who to tell and when.
Many kids live in two homes, and real friends understand.
No. You never have to choose between your grown-ups.
You can love both homes and both grown-ups.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you about school.
Many kids stay at the same school.

questionButtons.text: Why do I feel so sad?
fallbackAnswer: Big changes bring big feelings, and sadness is normal.
Telling a trusted grown-up helps the sadness feel smaller.

techniques.label: A colour calendar
techniques.how: Make a calendar with one colour for each home.

techniques.label: A travel bag
techniques.how: Pack a bag with special things that move between homes.

techniques.label: One toy for both homes
techniques.how: A comfort toy that always travels with your child.

techniques.label: Not your fault
techniques.how: Say often and clearly that it is not the child's fault.

techniques.label: Keeping in touch
techniques.how: Agree how the child can call or send pictures to the other grown-up.

techniques.label: A special spot in each home
techniques.how: Let your child set up a spot in each home.

techniques.label: Drawing feelings
techniques.how: Draw or colour feelings, and talk about them.

techniques.label: Trusted grown-ups
techniques.how: Name trusted grown-ups at school and in the family to talk to.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Travel bag packed, toy in hand

Before bed, here is a story about a little bird called Wren.
Wren's two grown-up birds decided to build two nests.
One nest was in the apple tree, and one was in the tall pine.
Wren felt confused and sad.
Is it because I was noisy, she asked.
No, said both grown-up birds, it is a grown-up choice, not because of you.
We both love you, and that will never change.
Wren would fly between the apple tree and the pine.
Each nest had soft feathers and a little spot just for her.
Some days she was in one, and some days in the other.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.

Some things change, and some things stay the same.
[[CHILD]] can ask any question, and the grown-ups will answer honestly.

When parents separate, it is about their relationship with each other, not their relationship with their kids.
Kids cannot cause it and cannot fix it, even though many kids wonder about both.
Families with two homes are very common, and kids in them do well, especially when they feel loved by both parents.
Feelings can be mixed and can change from day to day.
[[CHILD]] can ask to see the schedule and help plan how things move between homes.
Many families have different rules or routines in each home; that is normal, and kids adapt.
Some families have new partners or step-siblings over time, which comes with its own feelings.
School counselors and family therapists help many kids with this.
It is okay to love both homes, or to prefer one sometimes, without feeling guilty.
[[CHILD]] can choose who to talk to about it, and who not to.
Switch days can feel unsettled; a short routine, like unpacking and a snack, helps you land.
Keeping a few duplicates, like a toothbrush and pyjamas, at each home makes packing easier.
Shared calendars or apps help everyone know the plan.
It is not your job to carry messages between grown-ups.
[[CHILD]] can keep a special item that always travels, like a journal.
Grief is a normal reaction to a family change, even when the change is the right one.
Feelings may come in waves, sometimes at unexpected times like birthdays or holidays.
Feeling caught in the middle is a sign to tell a trusted adult.
Talking to a counselor is a sign of strength, not of something being wrong.
[[CHILD]] can keep a feelings journal, or use a code word to say, I need to talk.
Having a voice in small decisions, like room decor or the travel bag, helps kids feel in control.
Predictable switch routines lower stress for everyone.
Keeping a copy of the schedule in your room or on a device helps.
Planning a fun ritual for arrival at each home makes switches feel less like goodbyes.
[[CHILD]] can write down questions to ask both grown-ups together.
